architectural_implications.after: Closed-loop controller with an explicit state-observation step feeding the next decision cycle, and success judged on the trajectory of system state over time.
architectural_implications.before: Open-loop pipeline terminating at 'implement'; success judged at the moment of action.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires persistent, queryable environment state and a decision loop that does not terminate on action; makes delayed reward attribution a first-class design problem rather than an afterthought.
architectural_implications.observation: Agents are commonly built as request->plan->act pipelines with no path back from the environment's post-action state into the next decision.

architectural_implications.after: Every surprise becomes a revision to an explicit causal map of goals, decisions, state, effects, other agents, and delays.
architectural_implications.before: 'Side effects' logged as edge cases; fixes applied where the symptom appears.
architectural_implications.consequence: Shifts work from reactive patching to model maintenance; introduces a standing artifact (the causal map) that must be kept current or it becomes misleading.
architectural_implications.observation: Unexpected consequences are handled as incident categories and patched at the symptom site.

architectural_implications.after: A grounded, interactive simulator that reproduces delay and feedback structure, used both as a rehearsal environment and as the evaluation substrate.
architectural_implications.before: Declarative instruction and static benchmarks as the mechanism for improving behavior.
architectural_implications.consequence: Higher upfront cost to build a faithful environmental model; evaluation becomes trajectory-based and slower, but surfaces policy-resistance failures static evals cannot.
architectural_implications.observation: Reliability investment goes into documentation, prompting guidance, and static eval sets.

architectural_implications.after: Account for total loop-level cost including induced retries, human review, and rework.
architectural_implications.before: Optimize cost per call, latency per request, tokens per task.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires instrumenting the loop rather than the request; some locally-attractive optimizations will be rejected as net-negative.
architectural_implications.observation: Cost and performance optimization targets unit-level metrics because they are measurable per call.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe incident postmortems from symptom categorization to causal-map revision, with the maintenance burden named as the real tradeoff against cheap slogan-level thinking.
article_ideas.audience: Platform, SRE and AI reliability engineers who own postmortems
article_ideas.based_on: 'Side effects' is a category error, not a property of the world
article_ideas.thesis: Labeling an unexpected behavior a 'side effect' or 'edge case' is an admission that the causal model omitted a node, and the corrective action is to add that edge to a standing causal map rather than patch the symptom site — which means accepting the ongoing maintenance cost of a model artifact, because an incomplete map reproduces the same illusion.
article_ideas.title: There Are No Side Effects: Treat Every Production Surprise as a Missing Edge

article_ideas.angle: Take the five-step planning pipeline apart and show what each step looks like once an explicit observation edge back into decision is added, including the persistent queryable state it requires.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework designers and applied AI architects
article_ideas.thesis: Frameworks that terminate at 'implement' cannot represent the consequence of their own action, so they cannot correct; the architectural distinction that matters is not workflow orchestration quality but whether an observed-state edge feeds back into decision-making, which makes delayed reward attribution a first-class design problem rather than an afterthought.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Pipeline Is Open-Loop by Construction

article_ideas.angle: Argue from the lecture-versus-simulator claim to a reallocation of reliability budget, then confront the fidelity objection: a simulator only teaches the system it models.
article_ideas.audience: AI evaluation and ML platform teams
article_ideas.based_on: Lectures and documentation do not change mental models or behavior
article_ideas.thesis: Declarative instruction and static benchmarks do not change behavior, while rehearsal against a responsive environment that surfaces delayed consequences does; therefore eval investment belongs in a grounded simulator used as a training substrate, accepting trajectory-level scoring that is slower and costlier but catches policy-resistance failures static evals structurally cannot see.
article_ideas.title: The Eval Harness Is a Flight Simulator, Not a Scoreboard

article_ideas.angle: Use the healthcare cost-containment case as the structural analogue, then specify what loop-level instrumentation looks like when the 'unit' is a model call and the downstream work is retries and human review.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders accountable for AI unit economics
article_ideas.based_on: Policy resistance: interventions that succeed on the targeted metric
article_ideas.thesis: Optimizing a unit-level metric in a system with balancing loops reliably raises the aggregate metric, so agent teams that tune cost per call, latency per request or deflection rate should expect total cost or quality to degrade outside their tuning window; the correct target is the loop-level quantity, which requires instrumenting the loop and rejecting some locally attractive optimizations.
article_ideas.title: Cost Per Call Is a Local Optimum and a Global Loss

connections.relationship: Optimizing a unit-level measure is the general form of an intervention that triggers a balancing loop raising the aggregate measure.
Both are grounded environmental models used to test policy before deployment; the simulator additionally claims to change operator mental models.
Reframes each unexpected production behavior as a missing causal edge rather than an edge case to be patched.
If other actors re-optimize against your policy, static evaluation sets systematically overstate the durability of an intervention.
Delayed loop consequences are the mechanism that makes near-term success and long-term failure look like different problems.

evidence_quotes.text: Open-loop thinking (Identify problem -> Gather data -> Evaluate alternatives -> Select solution -> Implement) is common but does not reflect how the world works.
The world operates in endless feedback loops where decisions change the state of the system, creating new information for future decisions.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent that acts on an environment whose state persists should carry an explicit state-observation edge back into decision-making; pipelines that terminate at action are open-loop by construction.
core_insights.insight: The standard planning pipeline (identify problem -> gather data -> evaluate -> select -> implement) is structurally open-loop: it never re-observes the system state after acting. Real systems are circular, where each decision changes the state and that changed state becomes the input to the next decision. This argues that an agent loop should be modeled as a controller with explicit state observation and re-decision, not as a one-shot pipeline that terminates at 'implement'.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Most agent frameworks are built as linear pipelines with a terminal action step. If the system being acted on adapts or reacts, that architecture cannot represent the consequence of its own action, so it cannot correct. Making observed state a first-class input to the next decision is the architectural difference between a workflow and a controller.

evidence_quotes.text: Policy resistance occurs when expert-backed solutions work in the near term but make the problem worse in the long term.
Policies designed to cut unit costs of drugs and procedures trigger balancing feedback loops that drive up total costs.
Administrative costs of prior authorization reach $35 billion annually in the US.

core_insights.generalization: Optimizing a unit-level metric in a system with balancing loops reliably raises the aggregate metric; the correct target is the loop-level quantity, not the node-level one.
core_insights.insight: Policy resistance: interventions that succeed on the targeted metric in the near term trigger balancing feedback loops that degrade the global metric later. The mechanism is that the local measure being optimized is only one node in a loop; optimizing it moves other nodes in the opposite direction.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Agent and platform teams routinely optimize local proxies — cost per call, latency per request, tokens per task, deflection rate — and then observe total system cost or quality degrading. Policy resistance names the mechanism by which proxy optimization produces that reversal, and predicts it will not be visible within the tuning window.

evidence_quotes.text: There is no such thing as a 'side effect' in complex systems; there are only effects.
Every decision has multiple consequences; leaders must map the full feedback structure before acting.

core_insights.generalization: Every surprise in a deployed system is evidence of an incomplete causal model; the corrective action is to add the missing node or edge, not to suppress the symptom.
core_insights.insight: 'Side effects' is a category error, not a property of the world: there are only effects, and labeling some of them 'side' effects is an admission that the mental model omitted them. Operationally this means an unmodeled consequence should be treated as a missing edge in the causal map, not as noise or an edge case.
core_insights.why_it_matters: In production AI systems, unexpected behaviors are typically filed as edge cases, guardrail violations, or incidents. Reframing each one as a missing feedback edge forces the fix to be a model revision (which nodes and loops were omitted) rather than a patch at the symptom site.

evidence_quotes.text: Traditional project management education via lectures does not change mental models or behavior.
Decades of research showing lectures fail to change mental models, while flight simulator practice builds robust intuition.

core_insights.generalization: Interactive environments that surface delayed consequences are more effective at changing policy than declarative instruction; the harness, not the doc, is the mechanism.
core_insights.insight: Lectures and documentation do not change mental models or behavior; only experiential simulation in a safe environment does, because it exposes the operator to the delayed and counter-intuitive consequences of their own decisions.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is an argument about where capability lives. If behavior change comes from rehearsal against a responsive environment, then the investment belongs in a grounded simulator/eval harness that lets operators (and agents) experience consequences, not in more documentation or prompt instructions. It reframes the eval harness from a scoring gate into a training substrate.

evidence_quotes.text: Causal Feedback Loop Framework
Goals of Other Agents
Maps goals, decisions, system states, and actions to reveal how decisions generate feedback that alters future conditions.

core_insights.generalization: When the environment contains optimizing actors, an intervention changes their objective landscape, so counterfactual evaluation must model their response rather than assume stationarity.
core_insights.insight: The causal framework explicitly includes 'Goals of Other Agents' as a component alongside goals, decisions, state, effects, and delays. This means a system's response to your intervention is partly driven by other actors re-optimizing against you, which is a distinct mechanism from physical feedback.
core_insights.why_it_matters: In multi-agent and human-in-the-loop deployments, the environment includes adversaries, users, and reviewers who adapt to the system's policy. Any evaluation that holds other actors' behavior fixed will systematically overestimate the intervention's durability. It also implies the harness must include adaptive counterparts, not static datasets.

evidence_quotes.text: Simulators help leaders experience the consequences of over-hiring, scope creep, and schedule pressure.
Managing workforce, schedule pressure, quality, and scope adjustments.

core_insights.generalization: Capacity added under schedule pressure in a system with a rework loop tends to be absorbed by the rework it induces; throughput gains require breaking the quality->rework loop, not adding more workers.
core_insights.insight: Simulators let operators experience the downstream consequences of specific managerial behaviors — over-hiring, scope creep, schedule pressure — that produce rework. The named failure pattern is that adding capacity under pressure degrades quality, which generates rework, which consumes the added capacity.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is a concrete instance of a rework loop that maps directly onto agent scaling decisions: adding parallel agents or retries under deadline pressure increases output volume, which increases defects, which generates rework that consumes the added capacity. It predicts that naive horizontal scaling under time pressure can leave throughput flat.

evidence_quotes.text: Policy resistance occurs when expert-backed solutions work in the near term but make the problem worse in the long term.
Policies designed to cut unit costs of drugs and procedures trigger balancing feedback loops that drive up total costs.
The world operates in endless feedback loops where decisions change the state of the system, creating new information for future decisions.

deep_dives.research_question: Can the signature of a balancing loop — near-term improvement on a targeted metric followed by later reversal of an aggregate metric — be detected in logged decision and outcome time series before the reversal completes, without a manual expert causal-mapping exercise?
deep_dives.topic: Detecting balancing feedback loops from production telemetry
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Can balancing feedback loops be detected from production telemetry rather than requiring manual causal mapping by experts?
deep_dives.why: Policy resistance is currently diagnosed after the fact by facilitated causal mapping. If the loop signature is detectable in telemetry while the reversal is still in progress, the diagnostic moves from a retrospective workshop to an online monitor that can halt or reverse a policy mid-flight.

evidence_quotes.text: Every decision has multiple consequences; leaders must map the full feedback structure before acting.
Causal Feedback Loop Framework
Maps goals, decisions, system states, and actions to reveal how decisions generate feedback that alters future conditions.

deep_dives.research_question: Given the causal components the framework names (goals, decisions, system state, effects, goals of other agents, delays), what is the minimal subset of observation channels an agent must retain before it stops selecting policies that reverse?
deep_dives.topic: Minimum observable system state for avoiding policy resistance
deep_dives.trigger_insight: What is the minimum set of system-state variables an agent must observe to avoid policy resistance?
deep_dives.why: There is no sufficiency criterion for what an agent must observe. Without one, teams either over-instrument (observing everything, drowning in state) or silently omit the one node whose feedback drives the reversal — which reproduces the 'side effect' illusion inside the agent's own perception.

evidence_quotes.text: Policies designed to cut unit costs of drugs and procedures trigger balancing feedback loops that drive up total costs.
Administrative costs of prior authorization reach $35 billion annually in the US.
Policy resistance occurs when expert-backed solutions work in the near term but make the problem worse in the long term.

deep_dives.research_question: When unit-level metrics (cost per call, latency per request, tokens per task, deflection rate) are optimized, how much of the local saving is absorbed by induced retries, human review and rework, and does the aggregate loop-level metric reliably move the opposite way?
deep_dives.topic: Loop-level cost accounting for agent systems
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Optimizing a unit-level metric in a system with balancing loops reliably raises the aggregate metric
deep_dives.why: Proxy optimization is the default because unit metrics are measurable per call. Policy resistance predicts the saved cost routes into downstream work; instrumenting the loop rather than the request is the only way to reject locally attractive but net-negative optimizations.

evidence_quotes.text: Management flight simulators allow leaders to test strategies in a risk-free environment grounded in decades of system dynamics research.
Decades of research showing lectures fail to change mental models, while flight simulator practice builds robust intuition.

deep_dives.research_question: How closely must a simulator's delay structure and feedback topology match the deployment environment before a policy learned in the simulator transfers, and how does the transfer gap scale with structural infidelity?
deep_dives.topic: Simulator fidelity and policy transfer gap
deep_dives.trigger_insight: How does one validate that a simulator's underlying model matches the deployment environment closely enough to transfer learned policy?
deep_dives.why: The claim that simulators build robust intuition is only as strong as the underlying model. Without a validation procedure against real outcomes, a team can master the game rather than the system, and an eval harness inherits an unmeasured transfer gap.

evidence_quotes.text: Simulators help leaders experience the consequences of over-hiring, scope creep, and schedule pressure.
Managing workforce, schedule pressure, quality, and scope adjustments.

deep_dives.research_question: Does adding capacity (headcount, parallel agents, retries) under schedule pressure increase rework enough to cancel the added throughput, leaving aggregate throughput flat while unit quality falls?
deep_dives.topic: Rework loops under capacity scaling pressure
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Capacity added under schedule pressure in a system with a rework loop tends to be absorbed by the rework it induces
deep_dives.why: Horizontal scaling under deadline is the reflex response to being late. If a quality-to-rework loop absorbs the added capacity, the correct intervention is breaking that loop rather than provisioning more workers — a decision that can only be made if throughput is measured net of rework.

open_questions.question: Can balancing feedback loops be detected from production telemetry rather than requiring manual causal mapping by experts?
open_questions.research_direction: Instrument a deployed system for decision-level and outcome-level time series, then test whether intervention responses show the signature of a balancing loop (near-term improvement reversing into longer-term degradation) and whether that signature is detectable before the reversal completes.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary presents causal mapping as a facilitated expert exercise and flight simulators as research-grounded artifacts; it gives no method for inferring loop structure from logged state and decision data.

project_ideas.based_on: Can balancing feedback loops be detected from production telemetry rather than requiring manual causal mapping by experts?
project_ideas.hypothesis: A balancing loop's presence can be detected in production telemetry from the divergence between a targeted local metric and its aggregate counterpart before the aggregate reversal completes, with detection lead time proportional to the loop's delay length.
project_ideas.measurement: Detection lead time (how far before the aggregate metric crosses back past its pre-intervention baseline the alarm fires), false-positive rate on interventions with no balancing loop, and fraction of reversals caught.
project_ideas.name: Balancing-Loop Sentinel
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a deployed system (or a faithful simulation with known loop structure) to log decision-level and outcome-level time series; build a monitor that tracks local-metric improvement against aggregate-metric drift and raises a warning when the pair diverges in the direction predicted by a balancing loop. Backtest on at least one historical proxy-optimization episode.

project_ideas.based_on: What is the minimum set of system-state variables an agent must observe to avoid policy resistance?
project_ideas.hypothesis: There exists a minimal observation channel set below which an agent's policy choice reverses in a known balancing-loop environment, and removing each channel degrades policy durability monotonically up to a threshold rather than gradually.
project_ideas.measurement: Probability of selecting a policy whose long-horizon aggregate metric is worse than baseline, per ablation condition; identification of the threshold channel set and its stability across seeds.
project_ideas.name: Observation Ablation Rig
project_ideas.poc: Build a simulated environment with a single documented balancing loop and a controllable set of observation channels (targeted metric, aggregate metric, delay estimate, counterpart behavior). Run an agent across full factorial ablations of the channel set, recording chosen policies and their short- and long-horizon outcomes.

project_ideas.based_on: Capacity added under schedule pressure in a system with a rework loop tends to be absorbed by the rework it induces
project_ideas.hypothesis: Adding parallel workers or retries under schedule pressure leaves net throughput flat once induced rework is counted, and throughput gains only appear when the quality-to-rework loop is broken directly.
project_ideas.measurement: Net throughput delta per unit of added capacity, rework volume as a share of total work, and the capacity level at which marginal throughput goes to zero; compare against the loop-breaking intervention.
project_ideas.name: Rework-Aware Scaling Bench
project_ideas.poc: Implement a synthetic task pipeline with an explicit defect-generation rate, a rework queue and a capacity knob. Compare three policies under deadline pressure: add capacity, tighten scope, and invest in defect prevention. Score each on net completed work per unit time and on rework volume.

project_ideas.hypothesis: Interventions that look durable against a static evaluation set degrade measurably once counterpart actors are allowed to re-optimize against the deployed policy, and the degradation is predicted by how directly the intervention targets the counterpart's objective.
project_ideas.measurement: Durability gap between static and adaptive-counterpart regimes, and correlation between that gap and the degree to which the intervention targets counterpart objective terms.
project_ideas.name: Counterpart-Aware Eval
project_ideas.poc: Take an evaluation set with fixed human or adversarial responses and pair it with a counterpart policy that adapts to the system's decisions. Score the same intervention under both regimes and compare durability over repeated rounds.

source.title: Systems Thinking for Leaders: Designing Solutions That Work

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: John Sterman
  • Channel: MIT Sloan Executive Education
  • Main topic: Systems thinking, system dynamics, and designing solutions that work in complex business environments
  • Purpose: To educate leaders on applying systems thinking principles and system dynamics tools to identify root causes of persistent business problems and design effective, sustainable solutions. Professor John Sterman introduces systems thinking as a core capability for leaders navigating complex business, social, and environmental challenges. He explains the phenomenon of policy resistance—where well-intended interventions fail or backfire due to unrecognized feedback loops and time delays—and demonstrates how tools like causal mapping and management flight simulators help leaders overcome open-loop thinking and design high-leverage interventions.

Topic Map

Introduction to Systems Thinking

  • Explanation: Mollie Laffin-Rose Agbiboa introduces Professor John Sterman, who outlines the webinar agenda and sets the context for why systems thinking is essential in complex, interconnected environments.
  • Key claims:
    • We live in an overwhelmingly complex world where everything is connected.
    • Slogans about everything being connected are not operationally useful.
    • Leaders need operational tools to understand how real systems behave over time.
  • Examples:
    • One-week executive courses offered at MIT Sloan.
  • Terminology:
    • Systems thinking
    • System dynamics
    • Policy resistance
  • Why it matters: Provides the foundational justification for moving beyond surface-level management tools into systems-level problem solving.

Policy Resistance and Open-Loop vs. Feedback Thinking

  • Explanation: Explains why well-planned policies often fail or backfire (policy resistance) and contrasts linear open-loop thinking with circular feedback-loop thinking.
  • Key claims:
    • Policy resistance occurs when expert-backed solutions work in the near term but make the problem worse in the long term.
    • Open-loop thinking (Identify problem -> Gather data -> Evaluate alternatives -> Select solution -> Implement) is common but does not reflect how the world works.
    • The world operates in endless feedback loops where decisions change the state of the system, creating new information for future decisions.
  • Examples:
    • Urban traffic congestion: building more roads makes driving more attractive, ultimately worsening congestion.
    • US healthcare cost containment efforts failing for decades.
    • Failed mergers and acquisitions destroying value for acquiring firms.
    • Bicycle commuting requiring constant feedback to stay on the path safely.
  • Terminology:
    • Policy resistance
    • Open-loop thinking
    • Feedback loop
    • Causal diagram
    • Side effects
  • Why it matters: Helps leaders recognize the flaw in their own mental models and understand why standard planning processes repeatedly fail.

Case Study: Healthcare Prior Authorization and Unintended Consequences

  • Explanation: Detailed systems analysis of healthcare cost containment policies (prior authorization, preferred drug lists, step therapy) and their unintended consequences.
  • Key claims:
    • Policies designed to cut unit costs of drugs and procedures trigger balancing feedback loops that drive up total costs.
    • Prior authorization causes care delays, disease exacerbation, preventable hospitalizations, prolonged stays, and higher mortality.
    • Administrative costs of prior authorization reach $35 billion annually in the US.
  • Examples:
    • Blue Cross Blue Shield and UnitedHealthcare cutting back on prior authorization requirements in 2026 after recognizing system failures.
    • Doctors spending time on appeals and paperwork instead of patient care.
  • Terminology:
    • Prior authorization (PA)
    • Preferred drug list (PDL)
    • Step therapy (ST)
    • Balancing feedback loop
    • Vicious cycle
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates how rigorous causal mapping reveals hidden vicious cycles behind seemingly logical cost-cutting policies.

Project Management and Management Flight Simulators

  • Explanation: Explores why projects are chronically late, expensive, and wrong, and introduces MIT Management Flight Simulators as experiential learning tools.
  • Key claims:
    • Traditional project management education via lectures does not change mental models or behavior.
    • Management flight simulators allow leaders to test strategies in a risk-free environment grounded in decades of system dynamics research.
    • Simulators help leaders experience the consequences of over-hiring, scope creep, and schedule pressure.
  • Examples:
    • MIT Project Management Game simulating construction, hardware, and software projects.
    • Managing workforce, schedule pressure, quality, and scope adjustments.
  • Terminology:
    • Management flight simulator
    • High-level design
    • Detailed design
    • Rework
    • Management pressure
  • Why it matters: Bridges the gap between theory and practice by letting leaders learn system dynamics through direct simulation experience.

Key Points

Policy Resistance

  • Explanation: Well-intended interventions frequently fail because complex systems adapt and push back against changes, restoring the initial state or making conditions worse.
  • Evidence: Traffic congestion increasing despite road expansion; healthcare costs rising despite 70 years of cost-containment policies.
  • Practical implication: Leaders must anticipate systemic counter-reactions rather than assuming direct, linear cause-and-effect outcomes.

The Illusion of Side Effects

  • Explanation: There is no such thing as a 'side effect' in complex systems; there are only effects. Labeling consequences as side effects masks inadequate mental models.
  • Evidence: Sir Thomas More's Utopia (1516) describing remedies to one sore provoking another.
  • Practical implication: Every decision has multiple consequences; leaders must map the full feedback structure before acting.

Experiential Learning via Simulators

  • Explanation: Telling people what to do does not change behavior. Experiential simulation in safe environments builds genuine systems thinking capabilities.
  • Evidence: Decades of research showing lectures fail to change mental models, while flight simulator practice builds robust intuition.
  • Practical implication: Organizations should utilize interactive flight simulators for leadership training and strategy testing.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Causal Feedback Loop Framework

  • How it works: Maps goals, decisions, system states, and actions to reveal how decisions generate feedback that alters future conditions.
  • Components:
    • Goals
    • Decisions
    • State of the System
    • Side Effects / Multiple Effects
    • Goals of Other Agents
    • Delays
  • When to use: When diagnosing complex business problems where linear thinking has led to policy resistance.

Open-Loop vs. Feedback-Loop Mental Models

  • How it works: Contrasts linear step-by-step project execution models with circular, continuous feedback systems.
  • Components:
    • Identify Problem
    • Gather Data
    • Evaluate Alternatives
    • Select Solution
    • Implement
    • Feedback Loops
  • When to use: When designing project management workflows or strategic planning processes.

Examples & Case Studies

Cities built more roads to alleviate traffic congestion.

  • Illustrates: Policy resistance in urban planning.
  • Lesson: Making driving easier induces more driving and suburban sprawl, ultimately worsening congestion.

Health plans implemented prior authorization, preferred drug lists, and step therapy to cut costs.

  • Illustrates: Unintended consequences in healthcare management.
  • Lesson: Cost-containment policies increased administrative burdens, delayed care, worsened health outcomes, and drove total costs higher.

A project manager managing a hardware product in the MIT Project Management Simulator added workforce and pushed schedule pressure.

  • Illustrates:
  • Lesson: Pressure to cut corners and rush high-level design leads to massive rework, poor quality, budget overruns, and project failure.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Move beyond open-loop linear thinking to map feedback loops and delays in your projects.
    • Examine your organization's policies for potential policy resistance and balancing feedback loops.
  • Strategic:
    • Incorporate simulation tools and group modeling to challenge executive mental models safely.
    • Engage diverse stakeholders ('get the system in the room') to uncover hidden systemic perspectives.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • What are the unintended consequences of our current cost-cutting or efficiency initiatives?
    • How do our mental models of our business ecosystem differ from reality?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Healthcare administrative costs for prior authorization are $35 billion annually in the US ($11,000 per clinician). (statistical)
  • A 2026 systematic review of 25 studies showed prior authorization requirements were associated with disease exacerbation and preventable hospitalizations. (empirical research)

Notable Quotes

"And it will fall out as a complication of diseases, that by applying a remedy to one sore, you will provoke another; and that which removes the one ill symptom produces others...." (at 23:29) "All models are wrong, some models are useful." (at 77:11)

Compressed Summary

  • Systems thinking addresses policy resistance caused by mismatched mental models and complex feedback loops.

## Overview
- **Speaker**: John Sterman
- **Channel**: MIT Sloan Executive Education
- **Main topic**: Systems thinking, system dynamics, and designing solutions that work in complex business environments
- **Purpose**: To educate leaders on applying systems thinking principles and system dynamics tools to identify root causes of persistent business problems and design effective, sustainable solutions.
Professor John Sterman introduces systems thinking as a core capability for leaders navigating complex business, social, and environmental challenges. He explains the phenomenon of policy resistance—where well-intended interventions fail or backfire due to unrecognized feedback loops and time delays—and demonstrates how tools like causal mapping and management flight simulators help leaders overcome open-loop thinking and design high-leverage interventions.
## Topic Map
### Introduction to Systems Thinking
- **Explanation**: Mollie Laffin-Rose Agbiboa introduces Professor John Sterman, who outlines the webinar agenda and sets the context for why systems thinking is essential in complex, interconnected environments.
- **Key claims**:
  - We live in an overwhelmingly complex world where everything is connected.
  - Slogans about everything being connected are not operationally useful.
  - Leaders need operational tools to understand how real systems behave over time.
- **Examples**:
  - One-week executive courses offered at MIT Sloan.
- **Terminology**:
  - Systems thinking
  - System dynamics
  - Policy resistance
- **Why it matters**: Provides the foundational justification for moving beyond surface-level management tools into systems-level problem solving.
### Policy Resistance and Open-Loop vs. Feedback Thinking
- **Explanation**: Explains why well-planned policies often fail or backfire (policy resistance) and contrasts linear open-loop thinking with circular feedback-loop thinking.
- **Key claims**:
  - Policy resistance occurs when expert-backed solutions work in the near term but make the problem worse in the long term.
  - Open-loop thinking (Identify problem -> Gather data -> Evaluate alternatives -> Select solution -> Implement) is common but does not reflect how the world works.
  - The world operates in endless feedback loops where decisions change the state of the system, creating new information for future decisions.
- **Examples**:
  - Urban traffic congestion: building more roads makes driving more attractive, ultimately worsening congestion.
  - US healthcare cost containment efforts failing for decades.
  - Failed mergers and acquisitions destroying value for acquiring firms.
  - Bicycle commuting requiring constant feedback to stay on the path safely.
- **Terminology**:
  - Policy resistance
  - Open-loop thinking
  - Feedback loop
  - Causal diagram
  - Side effects
- **Why it matters**: Helps leaders recognize the flaw in their own mental models and understand why standard planning processes repeatedly fail.
### Case Study: Healthcare Prior Authorization and Unintended Consequences
- **Explanation**: Detailed systems analysis of healthcare cost containment policies (prior authorization, preferred drug lists, step therapy) and their unintended consequences.
- **Key claims**:
  - Policies designed to cut unit costs of drugs and procedures trigger balancing feedback loops that drive up total costs.
  - Prior authorization causes care delays, disease exacerbation, preventable hospitalizations, prolonged stays, and higher mortality.
  - Administrative costs of prior authorization reach $35 billion annually in the US.
- **Examples**:
  - Blue Cross Blue Shield and UnitedHealthcare cutting back on prior authorization requirements in 2026 after recognizing system failures.
  - Doctors spending time on appeals and paperwork instead of patient care.
- **Terminology**:
  - Prior authorization (PA)
  - Preferred drug list (PDL)
  - Step therapy (ST)
  - Balancing feedback loop
  - Vicious cycle
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates how rigorous causal mapping reveals hidden vicious cycles behind seemingly logical cost-cutting policies.
### Project Management and Management Flight Simulators
- **Explanation**: Explores why projects are chronically late, expensive, and wrong, and introduces MIT Management Flight Simulators as experiential learning tools.
- **Key claims**:
  - Traditional project management education via lectures does not change mental models or behavior.
  - Management flight simulators allow leaders to test strategies in a risk-free environment grounded in decades of system dynamics research.
  - Simulators help leaders experience the consequences of over-hiring, scope creep, and schedule pressure.
- **Examples**:
  - MIT Project Management Game simulating construction, hardware, and software projects.
  - Managing workforce, schedule pressure, quality, and scope adjustments.
- **Terminology**:
  - Management flight simulator
  - High-level design
  - Detailed design
  - Rework
  - Management pressure
- **Why it matters**: Bridges the gap between theory and practice by letting leaders learn system dynamics through direct simulation experience.
## Key Points
### Policy Resistance
- **Explanation**: Well-intended interventions frequently fail because complex systems adapt and push back against changes, restoring the initial state or making conditions worse.
- **Evidence**: Traffic congestion increasing despite road expansion; healthcare costs rising despite 70 years of cost-containment policies.
- **Practical implication**: Leaders must anticipate systemic counter-reactions rather than assuming direct, linear cause-and-effect outcomes.
### The Illusion of Side Effects
- **Explanation**: There is no such thing as a 'side effect' in complex systems; there are only effects. Labeling consequences as side effects masks inadequate mental models.
- **Evidence**: Sir Thomas More's Utopia (1516) describing remedies to one sore provoking another.
- **Practical implication**: Every decision has multiple consequences; leaders must map the full feedback structure before acting.
### Experiential Learning via Simulators
- **Explanation**: Telling people what to do does not change behavior. Experiential simulation in safe environments builds genuine systems thinking capabilities.
- **Evidence**: Decades of research showing lectures fail to change mental models, while flight simulator practice builds robust intuition.
- **Practical implication**: Organizations should utilize interactive flight simulators for leadership training and strategy testing.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Causal Feedback Loop Framework
- **How it works**: Maps goals, decisions, system states, and actions to reveal how decisions generate feedback that alters future conditions.
- **Components**:
  - Goals
  - Decisions
  - State of the System
  - Side Effects / Multiple Effects
  - Goals of Other Agents
  - Delays
- **When to use**: When diagnosing complex business problems where linear thinking has led to policy resistance.
### Open-Loop vs. Feedback-Loop Mental Models
- **How it works**: Contrasts linear step-by-step project execution models with circular, continuous feedback systems.
- **Components**:
  - Identify Problem
  - Gather Data
  - Evaluate Alternatives
  - Select Solution
  - Implement
  - Feedback Loops
- **When to use**: When designing project management workflows or strategic planning processes.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Cities built more roads to alleviate traffic congestion.
- **Illustrates**: Policy resistance in urban planning.
- **Lesson**: Making driving easier induces more driving and suburban sprawl, ultimately worsening congestion.
### Health plans implemented prior authorization, preferred drug lists, and step therapy to cut costs.
- **Illustrates**: Unintended consequences in healthcare management.
- **Lesson**: Cost-containment policies increased administrative burdens, delayed care, worsened health outcomes, and drove total costs higher.
### A project manager managing a hardware product in the MIT Project Management Simulator added workforce and pushed schedule pressure.
- **Illustrates**: 
- **Lesson**: Pressure to cut corners and rush high-level design leads to massive rework, poor quality, budget overruns, and project failure.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Move beyond open-loop linear thinking to map feedback loops and delays in your projects.
  - Examine your organization's policies for potential policy resistance and balancing feedback loops.
- **Strategic**:
  - Incorporate simulation tools and group modeling to challenge executive mental models safely.
  - Engage diverse stakeholders ('get the system in the room') to uncover hidden systemic perspectives.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - What are the unintended consequences of our current cost-cutting or efficiency initiatives?
  - How do our mental models of our business ecosystem differ from reality?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Healthcare administrative costs for prior authorization are $35 billion annually in the US ($11,000 per clinician). (statistical)
- A 2026 systematic review of 25 studies showed prior authorization requirements were associated with disease exacerbation and preventable hospitalizations. (empirical research)
## Notable Quotes
> "And it will fall out as a complication of diseases, that by applying a remedy to one sore, you will provoke another; and that which removes the one ill symptom produces others...." (at 23:29)
> "All models are wrong, some models are useful." (at 77:11)
## Compressed Summary
- Systems thinking addresses policy resistance caused by mismatched mental models and complex feedback loops.
- Linear open-loop planning fails in complex environments; leaders must account for feedback and time delays.
- Healthcare prior authorization illustrates how cost-cutting policies create vicious cycles that increase total costs.
- MIT management flight simulators provide risk-free experiential learning to build robust systems thinking skills.
- **Keywords**: systems thinking, system dynamics, policy resistance, feedback loops, flight simulator
- **Core insight**: Leaders fail when they apply linear, open-loop mental models to complex systems governed by feedback loops and time delays, generating severe policy resistance and unintended consequences.
